Standard Description: Understanding the organization and its context
rationale: Context Analysis has the organization document the internal factors, such as culture and technology, and external factors, such as threats and law, that shape its AI work. That record is the determination of internal and external issues Clause 4.1 asks for, and the documented analysis serves as audit evidence.

Standard Description: Understanding the organization and its context
rationale: Under the Records requirement, the organization keeps a context register along with minutes from the meetings where it is reviewed. An auditor can use the register and minutes as evidence that issues under Clause 4.1 were identified and revisited. Partial: the requirement keeps records but does not itself define how issues are determined or how AI roles are considered.

Standard Description: Understanding the organization and its context
rationale: Change Monitoring requires the organization to track new and changing regulations and then update its obligations and controls to match. This feeds the external legal issues that Clause 4.1 expects the organization to determine, and the regulatory tracking log shows they are kept current. Partial: it covers only legal and regulatory issues, not culture, technology, market, or AI role factors.

Standard Description: Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties
rationale: Feedback Loops set up channels so marginalized or impacted communities can comment directly on model performance and cultural relevance. The feedback collected shows Clause 4.2 needs and expectations of one group of interested parties being gathered. Partial: it does not produce a full list of interested parties or decide which of their requirements the AIMS will address.

Standard Description: Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties
rationale: Stakeholder Engagement brings affected groups and domain experts into reviews of high impact AI systems. Their participation records show the organization learning the needs and expectations of relevant parties under Clause 4.2. Partial: engagement is limited to high impact reviews and does not establish a register of all interested parties or record which requirements are addressed.

Standard Description: Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties
rationale: With Change Monitoring, the organization follows regulatory developments and revises its obligations and controls accordingly. Regulators are interested parties, so the obligations log evidences part of the requirements determination in Clause 4.2. Partial: it addresses only legal requirements and does not identify other interested parties such as customers, users, or affected communities.

Standard Description: Determining the scope of the AI management system
rationale: Boundary Definition requires current diagrams and inventories that separate in scope from out of scope components and show trust zones and interfaces. These artifacts set out the boundaries and applicability that Clause 4.3 requires, and auditors can review the diagrams and inventories as the documented scope.

Standard Description: Determining the scope of the AI management system
rationale: Lifecycle Coverage requires the organization to declare which lifecycle stages it governs, from data and training through deployment, monitoring, and retirement. That declaration sets the applicability of the AIMS across the AI lifecycle, a core element of the Clause 4.3 scope, and the documented scope statement carries over directly.

Standard Description: Determining the scope of the AI management system
rationale: The Review Cadence requirement makes the organization reassess its AI scope and risk at least annually and whenever a material change occurs. The review records show the Clause 4.3 scope being kept current as documented information. Partial: it maintains the scope but does not define the boundaries or tie them to the issues and interested party requirements Clause 4.3 references.

Standard Description: Determining the scope of the AI management system
rationale: The Evidence requirement has the organization retain inventory exports, risk decisions, approvals, and change records for its AI scope. Inventory exports show which AI systems fall inside the AIMS, supporting the Clause 4.3 scope with documented information. Partial: retaining records does not itself establish the boundaries or explain how context and stakeholder requirements were considered.

The Integration requirement aligns AI policies with the organization's SDLC, security, and privacy policies. That alignment helps show how AIMS processes interact with existing management processes, which Clause 4.4 asks the organization to determine. Partial: it addresses policy alignment only and does not define, implement, or document the full set of AIMS processes.

Through the Resources requirement, top management allocates budget and staffing to meet objectives and address risks. Budget approvals and staffing plans evidence the Clause 5.1 commitment to make needed resources available. Partial: resourcing is one leadership element; it does not cover setting the AI policy and objectives or integrating AIMS requirements into business processes.

Roles & Authorities requires appointing leaders for security, privacy, resilience, and AI governance with documented responsibilities. Making those appointments shows top management directing and supporting people who contribute to the AIMS under Clause 5.1. Partial: appointments do not show leadership setting policy and objectives, providing resources, or promoting continual improvement.

Risk Acceptance sets a threshold above which top management must explicitly accept residual risk, such as exposures over $1M. Signed acceptance records show leaders personally engaging with AI risk outcomes, which supports Clause 5.1. Partial: risk acceptance does not cover setting the AI policy and objectives, integrating the AIMS into processes, or promoting improvement.

The Oversight Charter defines leadership responsibilities for approving policy, setting risk appetite, and reviewing performance. Those duties match the Clause 5.1 expectation that top management establishes policy and objectives and makes sure the AIMS achieves its intended results, and the approved charter is direct evidence.

Risk Reporting has the board or executive body receive quarterly reports on incidents, audits, risks, and performance trends. Report packs and meeting records show top management checking that the AIMS achieves its intended results, part of Clause 5.1. Partial: receiving reports does not show leaders setting policy and objectives or providing resources.

Leadership records its directives on resources, remediation priorities, and strategic shifts under Decisions & Direction. Those recorded decisions evidence Clause 5.1 commitments such as providing resources and directing improvement. Partial: the requirement records decisions but does not by itself show top management establishing the AI policy or integrating AIMS requirements into business processes.

Approval & Ownership places the AI policy under the CAIO and requires approval from the CEO and Ethics Committee. CEO approval shows top management taking part in establishing the AI policy, one Clause 5.1 element. Partial: it does not show leadership setting objectives, providing resources, integrating the AIMS into processes, or promoting continual improvement.

Policy Creation & Approval requires each core policy to state its owner, approver, purpose, scope, roles, standards, and enforcement, with endorsement from top management or oversight. Applied to the AI policy, the endorsement record and structure support Clause 5.2. Partial: it is a generic policy standard and does not require the AI specific commitments to applicable requirements and continual improvement.

Version Control & Review requires policy versioning, approval logs, and annual reviews. These keep the AI policy available and current as documented information, and the approval log evidences that top management still endorses it under Clause 5.2. Partial: it controls the document but says nothing about the policy's required content or commitments.

Policy Components set the content of the AI policy, covering data governance, model development, transparency, human oversight, fairness, explainability, robustness, and lifecycle monitoring. The resulting policy document supplies the substance Clause 5.2 expects to be appropriate to the organization's purpose. Partial: the list does not require commitments to applicable requirements and continual improvement or a framework for setting AI objectives.

Approval & Ownership has the CAIO own the AI policy while the CEO and Ethics Committee approve it. The approval record shows top management establishing the policy, as Clause 5.2 requires. Partial: approval alone does not ensure the policy contains the required commitments, a framework for objectives, or communication to relevant parties.

Under Change Management, the organization updates its AI policies when regulations or technology shift. The revision history shows the Clause 5.2 policy kept appropriate and maintained as documented information. Partial: it governs updates only and does not establish the policy content, the required commitments, or a framework for AI objectives.

Roles & Authorities requires top management to appoint leaders for security, privacy, resilience, and AI governance with documented responsibilities. The documented role assignments are the evidence Clause 5.3 asks for when top management assigns responsibilities and authorities for relevant AIMS roles.

Executive Attestation requires the Accountable Executive to formally sign off that high risk AI systems meet safety and governance requirements before deployment. The signed attestations show an assigned authority answerable for conformance, part of Clause 5.3. Partial: it applies only to high risk deployments and does not assign or communicate responsibilities across other AIMS roles.

Accountability Mechanisms assign ownership for ethical AI and require audit trails of that ownership. Named owners evidence part of the Clause 5.3 assignment of responsibilities and authorities. Partial: the scope is ethical AI only, and it does not address responsibility for AIMS conformance or reporting on performance to top management.

The organization makes the CAIO owner of the AI policy, with approval from the CEO and Ethics Committee. This assigns clear authority for one key AIMS document, which supports Clause 5.3. Partial: it covers a single ownership role and does not assign responsibility for AIMS conformance and performance reporting or show roles being communicated.

Escalation Authority empowers the Ethics Oversight Committee to halt deployments until ethical risks are resolved. The committee charter documents a specific authority assigned by the organization, which Clause 5.3 asks top management to define. Partial: it grants one authority to one body and does not cover the broader set of AIMS roles or performance reporting.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: The AI Risk Framework defines the risk categories the organization assesses: ethical, technical, data, security, regulatory, and societal. This sets the scope of AI risk criteria that the Clause 6.1 planning process relies on, and the framework document is evidence for 6.1.1 and 6.1.2.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: The organization maintains an AI risk register recording each risk's tier, mitigations, owner, and validation outcomes. The register captures the outputs of AI risk assessment and treatment within Clause 6.1, so auditors can trace identified risks to chosen treatments and owners.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: Lifecycle Risk Assessments require risk assessments at design, data, training, deployment, operation, and retirement. Clause 6.1 planning depends on AI risks being identified and assessed, and the assessment reports from each lifecycle stage are direct evidence of that work.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: Results from testing, evaluation, verification, and validation are folded into the organization's risk analysis under the TEVV integration requirement. Test reports then inform likelihood and impact estimates, which strengthens the analysis step within Clause 6.1. Partial: it feeds analysis only and does not cover risk criteria, treatment selection, or impact assessment.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: Impact Assessment requires evaluating effects on rights, discrimination, safety, economic interests, the environment, and trust. Clause 6.1 includes AI system impact assessment as one of its planning activities, and the completed impact assessments are direct evidence for that part.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: Mitigation Planning has the organization define safeguards for identified impacts and disclose residual risks. This is the treatment step that Clause 6.1 plans for, and the mitigation plans and residual risk disclosures serve as treatment evidence.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: The AI Risk Framework requirement has the organization define risk categories covering ethical, technical, security, privacy, and societal impacts. These categories form the basis for the AI risk criteria Clause 6.1 asks the organization to set, and the framework document carries over as evidence.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: The AI Risk Register requires a central register tracking each risk's tier, likelihood and impact, mitigation plan, and owner. Within Clause 6.1, the register records assessment results and treatment plans, giving auditors one source to trace risks from identification to treatment.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: Lifecycle Risk Assessments call for assessing risk at design, data selection, training, deployment, operation, and retirement. The resulting assessments show the organization identifying and evaluating AI risks throughout the lifecycle, the core activity Clause 6.1 plans for.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities
rationale: TEVV Alignment folds testing, evaluation, verification, and validation results into the organization's risk calculations. The linked test results support the analysis portion of Clause 6.1 with measured evidence. Partial: it contributes to analysis but does not set risk criteria, select treatments, or assess impacts on individuals and society.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities: General
rationale: The Risk-Appetite Statement sets residual risk thresholds approved by the board. Clause 6.1.1 requires AI risk criteria that distinguish acceptable from non acceptable risk, and the approved statement provides exactly that threshold as documented evidence.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities: General
rationale: Delegation of Authority defines tiers of who may approve risk acceptance at each level. These approval tiers support the Clause 6.1.1 risk criteria by making clear how accepted risks are authorized. Partial: it governs acceptance decisions only and does not determine the risks and opportunities to be addressed.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities: General
rationale: The AI Risk Framework defines the categories of AI risk the organization considers, from ethical and technical to regulatory and societal. These categories help determine which risks must be addressed under Clause 6.1.1 and support the required risk criteria. Partial: it does not address opportunities or explain how the actions feed continual improvement.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities: General
rationale: Each identified AI risk is logged in the organization's AI risk register with its tier, mitigations, owner, and validation outcomes. The register is the documented record of risks determined and actions planned under Clause 6.1.1, and auditors can sample entries to confirm treatment ownership.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities: General
rationale: Risk Linkage maps each organizational objective to the specific risks and controls that affect it. The mapping shows risks being determined in relation to intended results, which supports Clause 6.1.1. Partial: it links existing risks to objectives but does not establish risk criteria or consider opportunities.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities: General
rationale: With the AI Risk Framework, the organization defines risk categories covering ethical, technical, security, privacy, and societal impact. The category set shapes which risks are determined under Clause 6.1.1 and supports the criteria the clause requires. Partial: opportunities are not addressed, and the framework does not distinguish acceptable from non acceptable risks.

Standard Description: Actions to address risks and opportunities: General
rationale: The AI Risk Register keeps a central record of each risk's tier, likelihood and impact, mitigation plan, and owner. That register documents the risks determined and the actions planned to address them under Clause 6.1.1, and sampled entries show owners assigned to each action.

Lifecycle Risk Assessments require assessing AI risk at each stage from design and data through deployment, operation, and retirement. That repeated assessment is the Clause 6.1.2 process applied in practice, and the stage assessment reports show risks identified, analyzed, and evaluated.

Under the TEVV integration requirement, testing and evaluation results become inputs to risk analysis. Test reports then supply evidence for the likelihood and consequence estimates used in Clause 6.1.2. Partial: it informs analysis only and does not define the assessment process, its criteria, or how results stay consistent and comparable.

Classification standardizes the likelihood and impact scales and key risk indicators used to rate risks. Shared scales are what let Clause 6.1.2 assessments produce consistent and comparable results, and the documented scales and KRI definitions carry over as evidence of the method.

Systematic Intake collects risks from threat modeling, red teaming, vulnerability scans, BIAs, DPIAs, supplier reviews, and TEVV. These sources feed the identification step of Clause 6.1.2, and the intake records show where each assessed risk came from.

Risk is reviewed quarterly under the Review Cadence requirement, with thresholds that trigger escalation. The review minutes show the Clause 6.1.2 assessment being repeated and evaluated against criteria. Partial: it sets frequency and escalation but does not define how risks are identified or analyzed.

Lifecycle Risk Assessments direct the organization to assess risk at design, data selection, training, deployment, operation, and retirement. These assessments apply the Clause 6.1.2 process across the lifecycle, and each stage report evidences identification, analysis, and evaluation of AI risks.

TEVV Alignment brings testing, evaluation, verification, and validation results into the risk calculations. This grounds Clause 6.1.2 analysis in measured performance data, with test results as linked evidence. Partial: it does not define the assessment process or the criteria used to evaluate risk.

The Risk-Appetite Statement sets board approved thresholds for residual risk. Those thresholds guide which risks need treatment and support the Clause 6.1.3 acceptance of residual risk. Partial: it does not select treatment options, determine controls, compare them with Annex A, or produce a Statement of Applicability.

Delegation of Authority sets approval tiers for risk acceptance. Approval records at the right tier evidence the Clause 6.1.3 step where designated owners accept residual AI risk. Partial: it covers acceptance only, not choosing treatments, determining controls, or producing a Statement of Applicability.

The AI risk register records each risk's tier, mitigations, owner, and validation outcomes. Recorded mitigations and owners evidence the treatment plan portion of Clause 6.1.3. Partial: the register does not show controls compared against Annex A or produce a Statement of Applicability.

Automated MLOps Governance Gates add policy as code checks to CI/CD that block deployment when risk requirements, such as a model card or bias threshold, are unmet. The gates implement selected treatment controls, and gate logs show them operating under the Clause 6.1.3 plan. Partial: they enforce controls but do not cover selecting treatment options, comparison with Annex A, or a Statement of Applicability.

Mitigation Planning requires defining safeguards for assessed impacts and disclosing residual risk. The safeguard plans form part of the Clause 6.1.3 treatment plan, and residual risk disclosures show what remains after treatment. Partial: it does not compare chosen controls with Annex A or produce a Statement of Applicability.

The Operationalization requirement ties each mitigation to TEVV checks, thresholds, and incident response. This puts the Clause 6.1.3 treatment plan into effect, and the linkage records show controls operating. Partial: it implements treatments but does not cover selecting options, comparing with Annex A, or a Statement of Applicability.

The AI Risk Register tracks each risk's mitigation plan and owner alongside its tier and likelihood and impact. Those mitigation plans evidence the treatment plan that Clause 6.1.3 requires. Partial: the register does not show treatment options weighed, controls compared with Annex A, or a Statement of Applicability.

Human Oversight requires documented escalation paths and named human controllers at decision checkpoints. These are treatment controls selected for AI risk, and the documentation shows them in the Clause 6.1.3 treatment plan. Partial: it covers one type of control and not the treatment process, Annex A comparison, or Statement of Applicability.

A Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) must be conducted and documented for high risk AI before deployment, covering privacy, non discrimination, and freedom of expression. This is an assessment of consequences for individuals and groups under Clause 6.1.4, and the FRIA document is direct evidence.

Impact Assessment has the organization evaluate effects on rights, discrimination, safety, economic interests, the environment, and trust. These are the consequences for individuals, groups, and societies that Clause 6.1.4 targets, and completed assessments are direct evidence.

Mitigation Planning defines safeguards against assessed impacts and requires disclosure of residual risk. These outputs show impact assessment results being acted on, which supports Clause 6.1.4. Partial: it does not define the assessment process or the method for evaluating consequences.

Pre-deployment Approval requires each impact assessment to be completed and approved before an AI system goes live. The approval record shows the Clause 6.1.4 process being applied at a defined point. Partial: it sets timing and approval but does not define how consequences are assessed.

Reassessment requires impact assessments to be revisited after major model or data changes or after incidents. Updated assessments show the Clause 6.1.4 process staying current as the system changes. Partial: it defines triggers but not the assessment method or the consequences to evaluate.

Adverse Impact Red-Teaming tests societal harm scenarios, trying to make the AI discriminate, spread dangerous misinformation, or infringe user rights. Red team findings validate impact mitigations and provide evidence for the Clause 6.1.4 assessment. Partial: it tests mitigations rather than defining the assessment process.

Through Review of PIAs/DPIAs, the Privacy Oversight Committee approves privacy risk and impact assessments for new systems. Approved assessments cover privacy consequences for individuals, part of Clause 6.1.4. Partial: privacy is one impact area, and safety, fairness, and societal consequences are not addressed.

Bias & Harm Review evaluates potential harm to protected classes, edge case populations, and contextual misuse. These reviews assess consequences for groups of individuals under Clause 6.1.4, with review records as evidence. Partial: they focus on bias and harm and leave out broader societal effects and the defined process.

Standard Description: AI objectives and planning to achieve them
rationale: The organization defines fairness metrics and thresholds for its AI systems. A documented fairness threshold is a measurable target that can support a Clause 6.2 AI objective. Partial: it covers fairness only and does not plan actions, resources, responsibility, timing, or evaluation.

Standard Description: AI objectives and planning to achieve them
rationale: Risk Linkage maps each objective to the risks and controls that affect it. This supports Clause 6.2 planning by showing what will be done to protect each objective. Partial: it does not make objectives measurable or assign resources, responsibility, timing, and evaluation methods.

Standard Description: AI objectives and planning to achieve them
rationale: Quantitative Gates set metrics for accuracy, robustness, fairness, calibration, and explainability coverage. These give measurable targets that can serve as AI objectives under Clause 6.2, with the gate definitions as evidence. Partial: the gates do not include plans for actions, resources, responsibility, or timing.

Standard Description: AI objectives and planning to achieve them
rationale: The KPI Framework defines standard KPIs and KRIs, such as model drift rate and bias index, aligned with strategy and risk appetite. These measures make AI objectives measurable under Clause 6.2, and the KPI catalog carries over as evidence. Partial: it defines metrics, not plans stating actions, resources, timing, and how results are evaluated.

Standard Description: AI objectives and planning to achieve them
rationale: Ownership & Accountability assigns an owner to each KPI and documents its calculation logic and data sources. Named owners and documented methods evidence the responsibility and evaluation elements of Clause 6.2 planning. Partial: it does not set the objectives themselves or plan resources and timing.

Under Change Management, AI policies are updated when regulations or technology change. Policy revisions are changes to the AIMS, and the revision record shows them carried out deliberately under Clause 6.3. Partial: it covers policy changes only, not other AIMS changes or how their consequences and resources are planned.

The Review Cadence requirement reassesses AI scope and risk on material change or at least annually. Scope revisions that follow these reviews are AIMS changes, and review records show them handled in a planned way under Clause 6.3. Partial: it does not address other changes to the AIMS or how such changes are planned.

Under the Resources requirement, top management allocates budget and staffing to meet objectives and address risks. This is the determination and provision of resources for the AIMS that Clause 7.1 requires, and budget and headcount approvals are direct evidence.

Decisions & Direction records leadership directives on resources, remediation priorities, and strategic shifts. Recorded resource directives evidence the Clause 7.1 provision of resources. Partial: it captures decisions but does not show resource needs being determined across the AIMS.

Resource Planning has the Security Oversight Committee approve investments in tools, talent, penetration testing, and monitoring. Approved investments show resources determined and provided, supporting Clause 7.1. Partial: the committee covers security resources and does not address the full set of resources the AIMS needs.

Competency requires education for directors on cyber, privacy, and AI risk. Training records show the competence of one group affecting AI governance being built, as Clause 7.2 requires. Partial: it covers directors only and does not determine required competence for other roles affecting AI performance.

Curriculum Design requires modular training on bias, fairness, explainability, data governance, TEVV, and legal obligations. The curriculum shows how competence is developed through education under Clause 7.2. Partial: it does not determine the competence each role needs or retain evidence that people are competent.

Assessment requires knowledge checks after training and retention of completion records. The completion and test records serve as the documented evidence of competence Clause 7.2 asks the organization to keep. Partial: it does not determine the competence required for each role affecting AI performance.

AI Lab Exercises put staff through hands-on simulations of prompt injection, data poisoning, and fairness audits. Attendance records and exercise results give Clause 7.2 evidence that people affecting AI performance gained competence through training. Partial: it does not define the competence each role needs or evaluate whether the training was effective.

Leadership Workshops run annual sessions for leaders on governance roles, risk appetite, audit duties, and regulatory trends. Under Clause 7.2, the session agendas and attendance logs show that leaders received education suited to their governance responsibilities. Partial: the workshops do not set out the required competence for each leadership role or check whether it was achieved.

Through Committee Orientation, new members of the ethics, privacy, and security committees receive onboarding decks. The decks and completion records support Clause 7.2 by showing that committee members are prepared for their oversight duties. Partial: orientation alone does not determine the competence each committee role requires or verify that members have it.

Independence & Competency separates builders from testers on high-risk releases and requires test engineers to hold AI safety and security skills. This defines needed competence for a role that affects AI performance, which is the first part of Clause 7.2, and skill records carry over as evidence. Partial: it covers only test engineers, not the wider set of roles.

The Training & Awareness requirement makes annual, scenario-based ethics training mandatory. Completion records and course content give Clause 7.3 evidence that staff are regularly reminded of ethical expectations that underpin the AI policy. Partial: ethics training is narrower than the AI policy and does not necessarily address each person's contribution to the AIMS or nonconformity consequences.

Ethical Framework Publication requires the organization to publish its AI ethics principles and what they mean in practice. The published principles give staff a reference point for the values behind the AI policy, which supports Clause 7.3. Partial: publishing a document does not ensure that people doing work are actually aware of it or of the consequences of not conforming.

The Accountability step makes managers responsible for team completion of AI training, with HR tracking compliance. HR completion reports give Clause 7.3 evidence that staff were reached by awareness training and that gaps are followed up. Partial: tracking completion does not show that the content covers the AI policy, each person's contribution, or the consequences of not conforming.

Curriculum Design builds modular training on bias, fairness, explainability, data governance, TEVV, and legal obligations. The curriculum shows Clause 7.3 auditors what staff are made aware of about responsible AI practice and their obligations. Partial: the listed modules do not explicitly cover the AI policy itself or the implications of failing to conform to the AIMS.

With Just-in-Time (JIT) Awareness Prompts, users and developers see in-application warnings when attempting high-risk actions such as uploading data to a public LLM. These prompts reinforce policy awareness at the point of work, and their configuration supports Clause 7.3. Partial: point-of-use warnings do not establish general awareness of the AI policy or of each person's role in the AIMS.

The AI-use disclosure requirement makes the organization tell users when AI is in use. Disclosure notices and their placement are evidence of a defined external communication under Clause 7.4, covering what is said and to whom. Partial: it addresses one external message and does not establish the broader internal and external communication plan for the AIMS.

The explainability statement requirement has the organization publish explanations for its significant AI systems. Those statements show Clause 7.4 auditors a determined external communication about how systems work. Partial: the statements are limited to system explanations and do not set when, how, or with whom other AIMS communications occur.

Transparency & User Disclosure obliges the organization to notify users when they are interacting with AI. Clause 7.4 accepts the disclosure notices as a determined external communication, specifying audience and content. Partial: this single disclosure does not address internal communication or the timing and channels for other AIMS matters.

Incident Reporting establishes procedures for notifying authorities of serious AI incidents. The procedure defines an external communication to regulators, including trigger and recipient, which supports Clause 7.4. Partial: it is limited to regulator incident notices and does not cover the wider set of internal and external AIMS communications.

Escalation Procedures set immediate escalation thresholds for critical risks and noncompliance events. The documented thresholds and routes define what is communicated, when, and to whom for urgent internal matters, which is one part of Clause 7.4. Partial: they do not cover routine internal communication or external communication about the AIMS.

Content Requirements specify that governance reports include risk posture, incidents, performance metrics, TEVV results, and trends. For Clause 7.4 this fixes the content of a key internal communication, and report templates serve as evidence. Partial: it does not determine the audiences, timing, or methods for communication, nor any external communication.

Communications & Notifications require notifying the Ethics and Privacy Committees, the CAIO, and affected customers or regulators when an AI incident warrants it. The notification matrix defines recipients and triggers for incident communications, which is part of Clause 7.4. Partial: it covers incident scenarios only, not the general communication needs of the AIMS.

Policy Creation & Approval requires each policy to name an owner and approver, state purpose, scope, roles, standards, and enforcement, and receive top management endorsement. This produces approved, identified policy documents, which is part of what Clause 7.5 expects. Partial: it covers policies only and does not address availability, protection, or retention of documented information.

Version Control & Review keeps policy versions, approval logs, and annual reviews. Version histories and approval logs show Clause 7.5 auditors that documented information is controlled when created and updated. Partial: the control applies to policies and does not extend to distribution, access, storage, or disposition of other AIMS records.

Under Change Management Integration, policy revisions pass through change control and risk assessment before taking effect. Change tickets for policy edits show that updates to documented information are controlled, which supports Clause 7.5. Partial: it covers only policy changes and says nothing about availability, protection, or retention.

Records Management requires traceability across data, design, and testing artifacts. Traceability links and the artifact records themselves are documented information the organization has judged necessary for its AI systems, which Clause 7.5 asks it to determine and control. Partial: it does not specify how those records are approved, protected, or retained.

Lifecycle Traceability links code repositories, data catalogs, MLOps registries, feature stores, and experiment trackers, and tracks model versions through deprecation and retirement. These linked records are documented information about each AI system, supporting Clause 7.5. Partial: the requirement establishes traceability but not review, approval, protection, or retention controls for that documentation.

Review Cadence requires a quarterly accuracy check of every inventory record and immediate updates after material changes. Review logs show Clause 7.5 auditors that the inventory, a key piece of documented information, is kept current. Partial: it does not address access control, protection, or retention of the inventory and other AIMS documents.

Availability & Backup requires the AI system registry to be highly available and its records and artifacts backed up. Backup schedules and availability reports demonstrate that documented information is available and protected, as Clause 7.5 requires. Partial: it covers the registry only and does not address creation, approval, or retention of other documentation.

Record Retention archives governance reports for at least three years to support audits. The retention rule shows Clause 7.5 auditors that one class of documented information is kept for a defined period. Partial: it does not address creation, approval, access control, or disposition, and applies only to reports.

Policy Creation & Approval has the organization write each policy with an owner, approver, purpose, scope, roles, and enforcement, then obtain top management endorsement. The approved AI policy and its supporting policies are documented information the standard requires, so Clause 7.5.1 is met directly by the policy set and its approval records.

Documentation Standards require standardized model cards covering metadata, purpose, inputs and outputs, provenance, metrics, and risk classification. Model cards are documented information the organization has deemed necessary for AIMS effectiveness, and the card template carries over to Clause 7.5.1. Partial: model cards do not cover the documented information the standard itself mandates, such as the AI policy or audit results.

Records Management requires traceable records for data, design, and testing artifacts. These artifact records are documented information the organization has determined it needs, which Clause 7.5.1 asks it to include in the AIMS. Partial: it does not address the full list of documented information that the standard explicitly requires.

The Risk & Compliance Fields requirement adds risk tier rationale, TEVV evidence pointers, impact assessment status, oversight points, and model card links to each inventory record. The enriched inventory is documented information that ties AI systems to their AIMS evidence, supporting Clause 7.5.1. Partial: it indexes some required records but does not itself establish the full documented information set.

Version Control & Review gives every policy a version number, an approval log, and an annual review. These map directly onto Clause 7.5.2, since versioning provides identification and the approval log records review and approval for suitability. Version histories and signed approvals carry over as evidence.

Change Management Integration requires policy revisions to go through change control and risk assessment. The change records show that updates to policy documents are reviewed and approved before release, which Clause 7.5.2 asks for. Partial: it does not address identification, format, or media of documented information, and covers policies only.

Review Cadence has each inventory record checked for accuracy every quarter and updated immediately after material changes. Clause 7.5.2 expects documented information to be reviewed for adequacy when updated, and the quarterly review logs provide that evidence for the inventory. Partial: it does not address identification, format, or formal approval of the records.

Version Control & Review keeps versioned policies with approval logs and annual reviews. Version histories provide the change control that Clause 7.5.3 lists among controls for documented information. Partial: versioning does not cover distribution, access restrictions, storage protection, retention periods, or disposition.

Availability & Backup keeps the AI system registry highly available and backs up its records and artifacts. Clause 7.5.3 requires documented information to be available where needed and preserved, and backup logs and uptime records meet that need for the registry. Automated MLOps Governance Gates stop model deployment when risk requirements, such as a model card or a bias threshold, are not met. Under I.TH-02 Monitoring, operational metrics are tracked continuously and alerts fire on threshold breaches. Clause 8.1 asks for processes to be controlled in line with criteria, and alert logs show deviations being caught. Partial: it covers runtime control only, not process planning, external providers, or planned changes.

Quantitative Gates define accuracy, robustness, fairness, calibration, and explainability coverage metrics. These metrics serve as the process criteria Clause 8.1 asks the organization to establish, and the threshold definitions carry over as evidence. Partial: setting criteria does not by itself implement control, cover external processes, or manage planned changes.

Standardized AI Lifecycle Stages define a common sequence from ideation through deployment to monitoring. Automated Policy Enforcement places Policy-as-Code gates in the CI/CD pipeline that block deployments missing test reports or failing security scans. Continuous Monitoring tracks drift, anomalous behavior, performance regressions, and data quality changes in operation. Partial: it covers the operational stage only and does not plan processes, set criteria, or manage external providers and planned changes.

Post-Market Monitoring calls for periodic reassessment of AI performance, fairness, and security after release. Partial: they focus on system behavior rather than a full assessment of AI risks against the organization's criteria.

Lifecycle Risk Assessments require AI risk to be assessed at design, data, training, deployment, operation, and retirement. Tying assessment to lifecycle stages gives Clause 8.2 the change-driven assessments it expects, and each completed stage assessment is a retained documented result.

Review Cadence sets a quarterly AI risk review with escalation thresholds. A quarterly review is a risk assessment at a planned interval, which Clause 8.2 requires, and the review minutes and updated risk ratings are the documented results to retain.

This requirement has the organization run AI risk assessments at design, data selection, training, deployment, operation, and retirement. Clause 8.2 asks for assessments when significant changes occur, and each lifecycle stage marks such a change. The stage assessment records are the retained results an auditor will sample.

The AI Risk Register records each risk's tier, mitigations, owner, and validation outcomes. For Clause 8.3 this is the core record: mitigations show the treatment plan is implemented, and validation outcomes show effectiveness was verified. The register itself is the retained documented result.

Automated MLOps Governance Gates block deployment when risk requirements, such as a model card or bias threshold, are unmet. Partial: gates enforce selected controls at one point and do not verify overall treatment plan effectiveness.

I.TH-02 Monitoring tracks metrics continuously and raises alerts on breaches. Alerts show whether controls are holding, which supports verifying treatment effectiveness under Clause 8.3. Partial: monitoring does not implement the treatment plan or document treatment results.

Quantitative Gates set metrics for accuracy, robustness, fairness, calibration, and explainability coverage. Continuous Monitoring tracks drift, anomalous behavior, performance regressions, and data quality changes. Partial: it does not implement treatments or record treatment plan results.

Under G.RM-03, AI systems are continuously monitored for drift, bias, and performance. Quantitative Gates define the accuracy, robustness, fairness, calibration, and explainability coverage metrics to track. Test Procedures sample TEVV artifacts, fairness and robustness metrics, privacy constraints, explainability proofs, and inventory completeness. The Follow-Up step confirms audit fixes work and revises the audit plan using lessons learned and incidents. The KPI Framework defines standard KPIs and KRIs tied to strategy and risk appetite, such as drift rate, bias index, and audit pass rates. These metrics supply the performance information that feeds the review under Clause 9.3. Partial: defining metrics does not itself make top management review the AIMS or decide on changes.

Content Requirements specifies that governance reports cover risk posture, incidents, performance metrics, TEVV results, and trends. The Oversight Charter assigns executive and board responsibility for policy approval, risk appetite, and performance review. The charter shows Clause 9.3.1 who is accountable for reviewing the AIMS. Risk Reporting delivers quarterly reports to leadership covering incidents, audit results, and trends. Decisions & Direction requires leadership to record its directives on resources, remediation priorities, and strategic shifts. These recorded directives are the documented results Clause 9.3.3 calls for, showing decisions on improvement and on changes needed to the management system.

Minutes & Records has the Ethics Oversight Committee retain evidence of reviews, decisions, and monitoring requirements. Continuous Improvement requires an annual review of metric relevance and the addition of new risk areas as technology changes. Lessons Learned feeds incident findings back into model risk management, training datasets, and detection rules. The Feedback Loop for reporting channels provides status updates, aggregates reports for trend analysis, and escalates systemic issues to risk committees. The audit Follow-Up step verifies that fixes worked and updates the audit plan based on lessons learned and incidents. Effectiveness checks and plan revisions are evidence of the ongoing improvement Clause 10.1 expects. Partial: improvement is confined to audit findings and the audit plan.

Root Cause & Post-Remediation calls for model lineage analysis after an incident and updates to training data, guardrails, or detection models. Standard Description: Assessing AI system impact on individuals or groups of individuals

Standard Description: Assessing AI system impact on individuals or groups of individuals

Standard Description: Assessing societal impacts of AI systems

Standard Description: Assessing societal impacts of AI systems

Standard Description: Assessing societal impacts of AI systems

Standard Description: Assessing societal impacts of AI systems
rationale: Mitigation Planning defines safeguards and residual-risk disclosures for the impacts an assessment identifies. Standard Description: Assessing societal impacts of AI systems
rationale: Adverse Impact Red-Teaming is built around societal harm scenarios, with testers trying to provoke misinformation, discrimination, or rights infringement. Partial: adversarial testing probes specific failure modes and does not replace a documented assessment of societal impacts over the system's life cycle.

Standard Description: Assessing societal impacts of AI systems

Standard Description: Assessing societal impacts of AI systems
rationale: The bias and harm review examines harms to protected classes, edge-case populations, and contextual misuse. Partial: the review centers on affected groups and does not address broader societal impacts such as environmental or economic ones.

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible development of AI system

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible development of AI system

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible development of AI system

Partial: accountability is one objective, and the requirement does not tie it to measures inside the development life cycle.

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible development of AI system

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible development of AI system

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible development of AI system

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible development of AI system

Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development
rationale: Testing & Validation requires bias, robustness, explainability, and performance testing prior to release. This defines the testing step within the responsible development process under Control A.6.1.3, and the pre-release test records carry over. Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development
rationale: Ethical Alignment adds fairness and inclusivity benchmarks and human-oversight checkpoints to development. Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development
rationale: Security/Privacy Integration requires secure storage, encryption, and privacy-preserving methods in AI development. Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development

Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development
rationale: Automated MLOps Governance Gates use policy-as-code checks in CI/CD to stop deployment when a model card is missing or a bias threshold is exceeded. Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development

Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development

Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development
rationale: Documentation Requirements oblige teams to produce model cards, data sheets, and fairness and robustness test reports. Standard Description: Processes for responsible AI system design and development
rationale: Automated Policy Enforcement places policy-as-code gates in the CI/CD pipeline that block deployments missing test reports or failing security scans. Ethical Alignment defines fairness and inclusivity benchmarks and human-oversight checkpoints. Intake Forms & Risk Evaluation make new AI initiatives submit an intake form with an ethical-risk evaluation. Partial: intake records the need and risk but does not amount to a full requirements specification.

Change Governance requires test evidence for change approvals and keeps traceability between requirements, risks, tests, and outcomes under a version-controlled QMS procedure. Partial: it manages requirements once they exist and does not require them to be specified for new systems.

Standard Description: Documentation of AI system design and development

Standard Description: Documentation of AI system design and development
rationale: Records Management requires traceability for data, design, and testing artifacts. Control A.6.2.3 asks that design and development be documented, and traceable records linking these artifacts are that documentation. The records repository and trace links serve as evidence.

Standard Description: Documentation of AI system design and development
rationale: Lifecycle Traceability links code repositories, data catalogs, MLOps registries, feature stores, and experiment trackers, and tracks model version transitions through retirement. Partial: it ties artifacts together but does not require design rationale or documentation against requirements.

Standard Description: Documentation of AI system design and development

These artifacts document how the AI system was designed and developed against its criteria, which is what Control A.6.2.3 requires, and they transfer directly as audit evidence.

Standard Description: Documentation of AI system design and development
rationale: Change Governance captures traceability between requirements, risks, tests, and outcomes under a documented QMS procedure. For Control A.6.2.3 this shows development decisions linked back to documented requirements, with the trace matrix as evidence. Control A.6.2.4 gains assurance that verification is performed objectively, shown by role assignments and competency records. Test Strategy & Coverage defines a risk-based strategy spanning unit, integration, system, and full-workflow testing, with negative tests, fuzzing, failure injection, and reproducibility tests for AI workflows. Test Oracles & Golden Baselines maintain golden datasets, expected outputs, and tolerance bands for numerical drift, all versioned. Change Governance requires test evidence before a change is approved and traces requirements to risks, tests, and outcomes. Partial: it applies V&V at change approval but does not define the measures or criteria themselves.

The Security Test Suite integrates SAST, DAST, IAST, dependency and container scans, secrets detection, adversarial AI tests such as jailbreak and prompt injection, and dataset quality tests. Risk Gates & Go/No-Go define validation gates tied to risk appetite and require executive or governance approval when results are marginal. This sets the criteria for using validation results that Control A.6.2.4 calls for, and the gate definitions and approval records are the evidence.

The validation Documentation requirement produces validation protocols, acceptance records, and the rationale behind each decision. That is the documented definition of validation measures and their outcomes under Control A.6.2.4, and the protocols and acceptance records transfer directly.

Tier-1 and high-risk AI must be validated in production-like conditions before general availability. Control A.6.2.4 gets a defined validation measure with a stated scope, evidenced by the environment description and validation results. Partial: it sets the testing environment for some systems but does not define acceptance criteria.

Operational Trials run staged rollouts or pilots under production-like load and validate performance, safety, explainability, and human factors. These trials are documented validation measures under Control A.6.2.4, and the trial plans and outcome reports carry over as evidence.

Partial: it covers human factors validation and does not define technical verification measures or criteria.

Executive Attestation requires the Accountable Executive to sign off that a high-risk AI system meets all safety and governance requirements before deployment. Automated MLOps Governance Gates prevent deployment when a model card is missing or a bias threshold is exceeded. Automated Policy Enforcement places policy-as-code gates in CI/CD that block deployments missing test reports or failing security scans. Control A.6.2.5 needs requirements confirmed before deployment, and gate logs prove each release passed. Partial: the gates check criteria automatically but there is no documented deployment plan.

Risk Gates & Go/No-Go define validation gates linked to risk appetite and escalate marginal results for executive or governance approval. Under Control A.6.2.5 the go/no-go record shows requirements were assessed before release. Partial: the gate decision is not a deployment plan covering rollout, environment, and support.

Tier-1 and high-risk AI must be validated in production-like conditions before general availability. That gives Control A.6.2.5 evidence that the system was confirmed to work in its target environment prior to deployment. Partial: it does not produce a documented deployment plan and applies only to higher-risk systems.

Operational Trials use staged rollouts or pilots under production-like load to validate performance, safety, explainability, and human factors. Minimum Metadata records purpose, intended and prohibited use, data sources, versions, evaluation metrics, endpoints, dependencies, and support terms for every inventoried system. Documentation Requirements mandate model cards, data sheets, and fairness and robustness test reports. Triage & SLAs sorts incoming reports by type, sets acknowledgement and response times, and tracks each one to closure. This transparency requirement commits the organization to tell users whenever AI is in use. Partial: it addresses one obligation to one party rather than a documented assessment of all reporting obligations.

Disclosures require notices to users that state known limitations and provide guidance for decisions. Partial: users are only one group of interested parties, and the requirement does not determine reporting duties to regulators, customers, or partners.

Standard Description: Processes for responsible use of AI systems

rationale: The threshold Monitoring requirement tracks AI metrics continuously and raises alerts when a threshold is breached. Standard Description: Processes for responsible use of AI systems
rationale: This oversight requirement has teams document escalation paths and name the human controllers responsible at each decision checkpoint. Standard Description: Processes for responsible use of AI systems
rationale: Continuous Monitoring requires tracking drift, anomalous behavior, performance regressions, and data quality changes in deployed AI. Standard Description: Objectives for responsible use of AI system

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible use of AI system

Standard Description: Objectives for responsible use of AI system
rationale: Thresholds & Alerts set tolerance bands for each KPI and trigger alerts when deviations exceed risk thresholds. Standard Description: Intended use of the AI system

Standard Description: Intended use of the AI system
rationale: Disclosures give users notices of known limitations and guidance on applying outputs to decisions. Contractual Clauses build security, confidentiality, data protection, and audit rights into supplier contracts. Monitoring & Renewal tracks vendor advisories, sets patch windows, and requires periodic re-attestation from suppliers. Shadow AI & Dependency Discovery scans developer environments and CI/CD pipelines for third-party AI models or libraries that skipped formal intake.
